t: The Gita is a dialogue between Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna, an avatar of Vishnu, at the start of the Kurukshetra War, and it forms part of the Mahabharata.
It brings together Vedic dharma, Sankhya-based yoga and knowledge, and bhakti (devotion), and teaches action without craving its fruits.
Tradition ascribes it to Vyasa, while scholars see a composite work, generally dated to the second or first century BCE, which has drawn hundreds of commentaries and readings.
dyk: Richard Davis cites a count by Callewaert and Hemraj in 1982 of 1,891 translations of the Bhagavad Gita in 75 languages, 273 of them in English.
ev: The Gita is generally dated to this time, though earlier and later estimates exist and 200 BCE may be the date of a major revision
Adi Shankara writes the oldest surviving commentary, which reads the text as teaching the non-dualism of Atman and Brahman
Ramanuja writes his Gita Bhashya, reading the text as qualified monism and Krishna's birth as physically real
Dnyaneshwar completes the Dnyaneshwari, a Marathi commentary and the oldest surviving literary work in that language
Charles Wilkins publishes the first English translation, with an introduction by Warren Hastings
Bal Gangadhar Tilak writes his commentary Shrimadh Bhagavad Gita Rahasya while serving a sentence for sedition
Gandhi's commentary, written in Gujarati in 1929 and translated by Mahadev Desai, is published in English
The Bhagavad Gita manuscript is added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register

f.made: Ascribed by tradition to the sage Vyasa; scholars regard it as a composite work of several authors or compilers
f.form: A Sanskrit poem of 700 verses in 18 chapters, mostly in the anushtubh metre, set within the Bhishma Parva of the Mahabharata
f.where: Manuscripts in many Indic scripts found on the Indian subcontinent, within the Mahabharata or on their own; the Gita manuscript was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in April 2025
f.known: The dialogue of Arjuna and Krishna on a battlefield; the teaching of selfless action; the three disciplines of knowledge, action and devotion; Krishna's universal form in chapter 11; commentaries by Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhvacharya; translations in many languages
